strengths: The core idea of designing discriminators inspired by nonlinear dynamical systems theory (Lyapunov exponents, detrended fluctuation analysis, recurrence, Poincaré plots) to capture chaotic/fractal properties of speech for bandwidth extension is a conceptually interesting and underexplored direction in GAN-based audio generation.

Reasonably extensive ablation studies (Tables 1 and 2) systematically probe the contribution of individual discriminator types and generator design choices (core block, inter-stream connectivity, depth, head count).

The paper reports parameter/computation efficiency gains (depth-wise separable convolutions, reduced discriminator size) alongside quality metrics, which is a relevant practical consideration for BWE deployment.

Comparison against several recent baselines (AP-BWE, MS-BWE, EBEN, AERO, NU-Wave) across multiple bandwidth-extension ranges and six objective metrics is a reasonably broad evaluation protocol in principle.
weaknesses: Figures are literally placeholders labeled 'Dummy' (Figs. 2/3) and Figure 1 depicts an architecture (Schrodinger Bridge, GTCB/GFCB blocks, three-stage Frequency/Phase/Time Generator-Discriminator pipeline with hierarchical multi-scale training) that does not match the text's description of the model (Lattice blocks, ConformerNeXt, MRLD/MSDFA/MRAD/MRPD discriminators). This makes the actual architecture impossible to verify or reproduce.

The abstract claims 'four new discriminators' but lists seven, including MS-RD and MR-PPD, which are never defined, implemented, or evaluated anywhere in the methodology (Section 3.2) or ablations (Tables 1-2) — a major inconsistency between claimed and delivered contributions.
The abstract claims a subjective evaluation with five human judges, but no methodology, protocol, or results for this subjective study appear anywhere in the paper.
Multiple citations in the Related Work section are broken/unresolved, appearing literally as '(?)', indicating the paper was not properly proofread or compiled before submission.

Key implementation details needed for reproducibility are missing or unspecified: delay-embedding dimension d and delay τ, epsilon values, tile size S, and training details for the additional un-ablated discriminators (MS-RD, MR-PPD); no code or data release is mentioned.

Numerical inconsistencies between text and tables (e.g., NISQA-MOS reported as 2.32 in Table 1 but 2.302 in text; other metrics given with more decimal precision in prose than in the corresponding table cells) suggest carelessness in results reporting.

Table 3, the main baseline comparison, has numerous empty cells for competing methods (NU-Wave, EBEN, AERO, MS-BWE), so the claimed 'new SoTA' comparison is incomplete and cannot be fully verified across all metrics and frequency ranges.

Framing of the '40x parameter reduction' by comparing MRLD+MSDFA against a completely different discriminator (MPD) is a misleading way to describe efficiency, since these are not compressed variants of the same component.

Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (VCTK, English only, noise-free), with no multi-lingual, cross-corpus, or noisy-condition testing, limiting generalizability claims despite the paper's framing as establishing a new SoTA paradigm.
No statistical significance testing, variance across runs, or confidence intervals are reported for any of the metrics, weakening the strength of the comparative claims.

Overall writing quality has frequent grammatical errors and typos (e.g., 'genertor', 'choas theory', 'supression', '05x' for 0.5x) that, combined with the unresolved figures and citations, suggest the manuscript was not carefully finalized before submission.

strengths: The core idea of using nonlinear-dynamics-inspired discriminators (Lyapunov exponents, detrended fluctuation analysis) as adversarial signals for BWE is conceptually interesting and, to the described extent, appears novel in the speech BWE literature.

The ablation studies that are actually reported (Tables 1 and 2) are reasonably systematic, isolating discriminator combinations and generator design choices (core block, connectivity, depth, DSC usage) with consistent metrics.
Reported parameter/computation efficiency (depth-wise separable convolutions, ~33.5M generator, smaller discriminators) is a plausible practical contribution if verified.
The paper evaluates on multiple frequency-extension ranges and reports six objective metrics, which is a reasonably broad protocol for the portions that are complete.
weaknesses: Fundamental completeness failure: Figures 2 and 3 are explicitly labeled 'Dummy' and do not correspond to the paper's content, meaning key qualitative/illustrative evidence is entirely missing or incorrect as submitted.

The abstract advertises four novel discriminators (MRLD, MS-RD, MSDFA, MR-PPD) plus MPD/MRAD/MRPD (seven total), but Section 3.2 ('Chaos-Informed Nonlinear Discriminator') only defines and evaluates MRLD, MSDFA, MRAD, and MRPD. MS-RD (Multi-Scale Recurrence Discriminator) and MR-PPD (Multi-Resolution Poincaré Plot Discriminator) — two of the four headline contributions — are never described, implemented, or ablated anywhere in the paper. This is a serious mismatch between claimed and demonstrated contributions.

The abstract claims subjective evaluation with five human judges as a key part of the evidence for 'new SoTA', but no subjective evaluation methodology, protocol, or results appear anywhere in the results section (Section 4) or elsewhere in the paper.
Multiple citations in the Related Work section are broken placeholders '(?)' (e.g., for Griffin-Lim and LPC-based methods), indicating the submission was not properly finalized.

The main comparative table (Table 3) has extensive missing values for baseline methods NU-Wave, EBEN, and AERO (blank cells across most metrics and ranges), undermining the comparative claim of establishing a new SoTA against the full baseline set.

Key reproducibility details are missing: delay-embedding dimension d and delay τ for MRLD are never specified with concrete values; dataset train/val/test split protocol is not described; no variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported for any metric.

The paper's central theoretical motivation (that generated speech lacks 'authentic chaotic dynamics') is never directly validated — e.g., no comparison of measured Lyapunov exponents or DFA statistics between real and generated audio to empirically support the core hypothesis; the argument remains largely narrative.

On SI-SDR/SI-SNR, the proposed model is described as giving 'similar' performance to AP-BWE and MS-BWE, but the actual numbers in Table 3 show AP-BWE outperforming NDSI-BWE on these metrics for two of three ranges (e.g., 18.26 vs 18.13, 20.86 vs 19.53), which is understated in the text.

Writing quality is poor throughout, with frequent typos and grammatical errors ('genertor', 'choas', 'benchmakr', 'supression', 'struggles') that impede clarity and suggest insufficient proofreading before submission.

No statistical significance testing is reported for any of the objective metric comparisons across models, making it hard to assess whether reported gains are meaningful versus noise given a single run per configuration.

strengths: Creative and interesting central idea: grounding discriminator design in speech's known nonlinear-dynamical/chaotic properties (Lyapunov exponents, detrended fluctuation analysis) is a novel angle on GAN-based BWE that differentiates the work from purely spectrogram/periodicity-based discriminators (MPD/MSD/MRSD).

Extensive and systematic ablation studies (Tables 2 and 3) isolating the contribution of each discriminator (MRLD, MSDFA, MRAD, MRPD) and each generator design choice (core block, inter-stream connectivity, depth, head count, DSC), which is good methodological practice.

Reasonably comprehensive evaluation suite: six objective metrics, two subjective protocols (MOS, pairwise preference), and three efficiency metrics (params, MACs/FLOPs, RTF), across multiple bandwidth-extension ranges and three baselines.
Detailed appendices with layer-wise parameter breakdowns, hyperparameter tables, and preprocessing/inference pipeline descriptions that partially aid reproducibility.
Efficiency claims are attractive if valid: notable parameter and computation reduction versus AP-BWE while reportedly maintaining or improving several perceptual metrics.
weaknesses: The Lyapunov-exponent estimation in MRLD (Algorithm 1) is applied to extremely short windows (64-1024 samples) with unspecified embedding dimension, delay, and evolution horizon Δ in the main text; such short-window, non-stationary segments make classical Lyapunov exponent estimation statistically unreliable, and the paper does not validate that the computed quantities are meaningfully capturing 'chaos' rather than arbitrary local signal statistics.

The term 'complex-valued' network/generator is used repeatedly but the actual architecture processes magnitude and phase (or pseudo-real/imaginary) via separate real-valued streams merged at the end rather than using genuine complex-valued layers (complex convolutions/complex arithmetic throughout); this terminology appears potentially misleading relative to the true architecture.

No statistical significance testing, variance, or multiple-seed reporting is provided for any of the numerous small metric differences (e.g., LSD 1.10 vs 1.09, PESQ differences of ~0.05), making many comparative claims ('better performance') difficult to substantiate rigorously.

Subjective evaluation is based on only 10 non-native, non-target-language listeners (Bangladeshi students rating English VCTK speech), which is a small and non-representative panel for perceptual claims about an English TTS/ASR-oriented BWE system; furthermore, the appendix text (A.9) describes results 'under noisy and reverberant conditions' and reports an '11%' preference margin in Fig. 4/main text versus a '2%' improvement figure in Appendix A.9 for the same comparison — this internal inconsistency suggests copy-paste from a different experiment/paper and undermines confidence in the reported subjective results.

The headline '40x discriminator-size reduction' claim (Table 2, row 11) rests on a single MPD parameter count (22M) that is unusually large relative to typical MPD implementations in the literature (~1-2M parameters), raising concern about whether this specific baseline configuration is representative/fair, which weakens the strength of this key efficiency claim.

Evaluation is limited to a single corpus (VCTK) and a single language (English) with no cross-corpus, multi-speaker generalization, or noisy/reverberant condition testing, explicitly acknowledged as a limitation but still constraining the generality of the claimed 'new baseline' status.

No code or model release is mentioned, and despite detailed architecture tables, several implementation specifics (e.g., MRLD's τ, embedding dimension d, ϵ, Δ) are only partially specified, which could hinder exact reproducibility of the proposed chaos-based discriminators.

The paper's novelty is primarily a combination of existing components (ConvNeXt, Conformer, LatticeNet, MPD-style multi-resolution discriminators, DFA/Lyapunov exponent features) rather than fundamentally new theory or method, so its contribution should be assessed as solid engineering integration rather than a conceptual breakthrough.

strengths: Introduces a creative combination of nonlinear dynamical-systems concepts (Lyapunov exponents, detrended fluctuation analysis) with adversarial discriminators for speech bandwidth extension, which is a novel angle relative to standard MPD/MSD/MRD discriminator families.

Extensive and systematic ablation studies are provided for both the discriminator design (Table 2, comparing MRLD/MSDFA combinations against MPD) and generator design (Table 3, core block, connectivity, depth, head count), which help isolate the contribution of each component.

Strong reproducibility support: detailed appendices document the dataset preprocessing pipeline, layer-wise parameter breakdowns for generator and discriminators, full hyperparameter tables, and inference workflow.

Comprehensive evaluation across six objective metrics, two subjective metrics, and three efficiency metrics (MACs/FLOPs/RTF), together with comparisons over multiple frequency extension ranges (4→16, 8→16, 16→48 kHz).

Demonstrated efficiency gains (roughly 0.5x parameters and 40x smaller discriminators than AP-BWE) while matching or exceeding several objective/perceptual metrics, which is a practically relevant contribution for on-device or real-time BWE.
weaknesses: The scientific grounding of the 'chaos-informed' claim is questionable: Lyapunov exponents are estimated from windows as short as 64–1024 samples (a few milliseconds at 16kHz), which is far too short for reliable delay-embedding-based chaotic invariant estimation per standard nonlinear-dynamics practice; no validation is given that the extracted quantities actually behave like genuine Lyapunov exponents or DFA scaling exponents (e.g., no sanity check against known chaotic vs. non-chaotic speech segments, no comparison to ground-truth chaotic indicators). This weakens the central 'deterministic chaos' narrative, even though the resulting discriminators do empirically improve GAN training.

No statistical significance testing is reported for any of the metric differences (objective or subjective), and several improvements over the strongest baseline (AP-BWE) are numerically small (e.g., PESQ 2.64 vs 2.55, STOI 0.95 vs 0.94), making it hard to assess whether gains are robust or within noise.

The subjective evaluation panel is small (n=10) and demographically narrow (Bangladeshi undergraduates, all non-native English listeners), limiting the generalizability of MOS and pairwise preference conclusions, especially for an English-language corpus.

Despite motivating the work heavily via TTS/ASR applications in the introduction, no downstream task evaluation (e.g., WER with an ASR system, or TTS naturalness with reconstructed features) is performed; all evaluation is intrinsic to the BWE/audio-reconstruction task itself, weakening the NLP-application relevance claims made in the abstract/intro.

Evaluation is restricted to a single dataset (VCTK), single language (English), and clean/noise-free conditions, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation; generalization to noisy, multilingual, or spontaneous speech is untested.

The relevance to core computational linguistics/NLP is somewhat tangential — the work is essentially a speech-signal-processing/audio-generation contribution (more typical of ICASSP/Interspeech) with only motivational links to ASR/TTS rather than demonstrated impact on language-related tasks.
No code/checkpoint release is mentioned, so despite thorough hyperparameter documentation, independent reproduction still requires reimplementation from the described architecture.
